title: The Land Remembers
subtitle: On Sacred Land and Mountain Worship in Mongolia
author: Nyamsuren Erdenebayar

runs.text: , the ritual offering of milk to the land, sky, and ancestral spirits, on the open balcony of a Soviet-era apartment building near the old airport in Ulaanbaatar. We lived so close to the flight path that the sound of engines overhead became the texture of my childhood. Whenever a plane passed, my grandmother took a spoon of milk and raised it toward the horizon, wishing the travelers a safe journey. This gesture extends far beyond safe travel:

is how Mongolians greet the morning, acknowledge the land beneath them, and maintain our relationship with the spirits of mountains, rivers, and sky. For generations, the female head of a Mongolian household has offered milk to the sky as an ordinary daily practice.

Nearly every Mongolian grows up knowing that the land is alive. It can be benevolent when honored, but also wrathful when disrespected. Cautionary stories would circulate matter of factly in casual conversation: someone mysteriously fell ill after urinating in a river or met sudden misfortune after digging sacred ground. Most Mongolians have heard of the existence of land spirits even if they don’t accept it as truth. I certainly never questioned the aliveness of land growing up. It was only when I left Mongolia and saw how rare this acceptance appears elsewhere that I felt the pull to understand what I had always simply known. runs.text: refers to one’s "homeland" or "native land.” Beyond just a geographical location, there is a spiritual sense to the word as well. Your

is the specific land that made you: the mountains your lineage has worshiped, the river your ancestors watered their horses in, the sky your family has read for weather and omens across generations. According to our patrilineal tradition, your father's
It is a place that chose you and has been in a reciprocal relationship with your ancestors long enough that the relationship itself becomes part of who you are.

is home to Otgontenger Khairkhan, one of Mongolia’s ten state-worshipped sacred mountains, and the one my ancestors have been returning to for centuries. Its name translates roughly as “Youngest Sky.” Its presiding deity is Ochirvaani, the fierce dark-blue Buddhist protector also known as Vajrapani, the holder of thunderbolt. The mountain is understood as Ochirvaani’s abode and living body.

runs.text: The practice of worshipping sacred mountains is documented as far back as the 13th century. The

records how Chinggis Khan declared Burkhan Khaldun sacred and vowed that his descendants would worship it for generations to come. This is how a state theology of sacred geography began to take shape. By the 18th century, Otgontenger Khairkhan was officially decreed a site of state worship under the Qing Dynasty. That recognition held through Bogd Khan's rule, was suppressed entirely under the Stalinist-era anti-religious purges in the 1930s, and was restored by presidential decree in 1995. State ceremonies now take place every four years with the president in attendance.

When we reached the mountain, the women stayed behind by the temple on a small hill while the men rode on horseback to the lake nested inside the mountain. After the monks complete the morning chants, the day opens into celebration. Any bad deed or unkind word is prohibited during land worship ceremonies. People arrive in their cherished/gangan traditional
the silk robes reserved for occasions worth dressing up for. The wrestling, horse races, children riding out across the steppe are all part of the offering. Joy is the highest offering of all.

runs.text: Some mountains you are born belonging to. Others you live into. That's how I found myself in front of Herlen Toono Mountain on the eighth day of the first month of summer, the dog day of the snake month, May 28th, 2026. In Mongolia, as across much of Asia, the twelve animals of the zodiac move across years, months, days, and hours. You check if the day is suitable before a haircut, a journey, a ceremony. The worship ceremony date is set the same way: an astrologer reads the moment, finding the alignment between human intention and the world's willingness to receive it.
The locals had gathered to venerate Herlen Toono, a mountain that sits near the Kherlen River which originates near Burkhan Khaldun, Chinggis Khan's sacred mountain. I arrived at the

, literally "wind horse," is one's inner spiritual vitality. It is represented by a horse carrying a wish-fulfilling jewel across the sky. It is strengthened or weakened by one’s actions, fortune, and relationship with the land and its spirits. If you have a strong khiimori, life is aligned and synchronicities find their way into your life with ease. And the opposite if your khiimori is low. Galloping on a horse is one of the best ways to uplift your khiimori.

runs.text: Before the jockeys took off, the horses were evaluated on breed and lineage. Only pure Mongolian breeds were allowed to race. Spectators chanted
the jockey song meant to encourage the horses and strengthen their relationship with the rider. In early tradition, the sweat scraped from winning horses was fermented into a celebratory drink called
, fermented mare's milk. A horse that places in the first fifth is said to have
. On a sweltering summer day, fermented mare’s milk is a staple out on the steppe.

runs.text: As we waited for the riders to return, the gathering turned into a lively reunion. Kin who had scattered to cities or abroad came back to the same valley, the same mountain, and took stock of each other. Someone's son had grown tall. Someone's father had aged. You reconnect with kin through celebration. The
is a scheduled return. The mountain sets the date and everyone who belongs to it comes home.

runs.text: At Herlen Toono, children ran between the
, rode horses bareback, and laughed with no restraint. Nobody called them to attention. Nobody asked them to watch. No one explained the
to them. They were just there the way children are there. Fully, carelessly, and completely.
I was there the same way. Herlen Toono was not my ancestral mountain, yet it welcomed me unconditionally. Belonging is not exclusive only to your

. As long as you remain in correct symbiosis with the land, it hosts you like you are their own. Land worship is ingrained in our language and rituals, not exclusively through worship ceremonies. The ritual of
survived purges and urbanization because it only requires the land and the people on it to remain in reciprocity. The land remembers. And so should we.
